entries.title: Opening Day for the Obamas, as Democratic elites gather for historic presidential center opening
entries.summary: <p>All eyes are on Chicago on Thursday, as top Democrats, operatives and musical legends arrive to celebrate Barack Obama’s namesake presidential center in the city where the nation’s first Black president launched his political career.</p><p>The former president and first lady Michelle Obama are back in their hometown for the culmination of more than a decade of planning, legal fights, political squabbles and blueprints for massive economic development that have led to the Juneteenth public opening of the Obama Presidential Center in Jackson Park.</p><p>A who’s-who of Chicago’s political elite will be on hand for Thursday’s dedication ceremony, which features an A-list musical lineup including Bruce Springsteen, Bono, Common, Eddie Vedder, John Legend and more.</p><p>Former Presidents George W. Bush, Bill Clinton and Joe Biden <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/06/17/obama-presidential-center-ceremony-former-presidents-bush-clinton-biden-attending" >will be on hand </a>along with former first ladies Laura Bush, former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton and Jill Biden at the center's John Lewis Plaza. The ceremony begins at 11 a.m. Thursday.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/arts-and-culture/2026/06/16/obama-presidential-center" >What to know about the Obama Presidential Center’s opening weekend and beyond</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>The A-list crowd will mean heavy security, which the U.S. Secret Service likened to a smaller scale security plan similar to the Democratic National Convention in Chicago in 2024.</p><p>Thousands are expected to attend a ticketed watch party on the Midway Plaisance, which opens at 9 a.m. Thousands are also anticipated at the dedication ceremony.</p><p>"There will be anti-scale fencing, vehicle checkpoints, magnetometers. We're going to have tactical assets there, some that are going to be publicly visible and some that won't," said James Morley, acting Special Agent in Charge of the U.S. Secret Service Chicago Field Office. "We'll have drone support for overwatch and there's going to be a temporary flight restriction in place that's going to restrict aircraft, as well as drones over the Obama Presidential Center."</p><p>The center officially opens to the public on Friday, capping a journey that started with Obama’s 2015 announcement that he would build his presidential center on the South Side, where he started as a community organizer and served as a state senator.</p><p>His namesake foundation faced pushback from community organizers who demanded community benefits agreements, while parkland advocates mounted lengthy court battles in a failed attempt to block construction of the eight-story building in the heart of historic Jackson Park.</p><p>The foundation broke ground in September 2021, promising it would be a “university for activism and social change.”</p><p>“This day’s been a long time comin’,” the nation’s 44th president told a crowd when he took to the podium in Jackson Park.</p><p>“Chicago is where almost everything that is most precious to me began,” the former president said, a rendering of his presidential center behind him.</p><p>The South Side neighborhood is where Michelle Obama grew up, where the former president started his political career surrounded by a “vibrant neighborhood and a community where we believe we can help make a difference.”</p><p>The neighborhood was also the former president’s “entryway into Chicago.” He told of driving here in the summer of 1985 in a “pretty janky” car, coming off the Skyway and driving through Jackson Park which was “a lot more beautiful than I expected.”</p><p>In 2021, Obama said the center would be a “living, thriving home for concerts and cultural events” and a hub for those who “want to strengthen democratic ideals.”</p><p>U.S. Sen. Angela Alsobrooks, D-Maryland, is among a long list of Democrats flying into Chicago for the opening. Obama personally called Alsobrooks after she won the Democratic primary in 2024, and helped to support her in her general election against former Republican Gov. Larry Hogan.</p><p>“He was like a coach. He sat me down. We talked, and he gave me really great pieces of advice, but one of the things he said to me was to guard against cynicism,” Alsobrooks said. “He said, ‘You will be inundated with all kinds of information. You'll be inundated with kind of the happenings of the world,’ and his advice to me was to really allow myself to remain in the place where I would be free of cynicism.”</p><p>Alsobrooks said the center’s opening during the second Trump administration is essential, because the country “needs to see each other as neighbors.”</p><p>“I think people need a reminder of what's possible, and they need to know why we are still hopeful,” Alsobrooks said. “When I think about his election, it's like it can never be erased. The significance of it can never be erased, not only his election, but his mere presence in that office.”</p>
entries.author: Mitchell Armentrout

entries.title: Tim Kowalski, mortuary science teacher who influenced generations of funeral directors in Chicago, dead at 75
entries.summary: <p></p><p></p><p>If you've attended a funeral in Chicago, you've probably witnessed the reach of Tim Kowalski's work.</p><p>Over the span of 30-plus years teaching at the Worsham College of Mortuary Science in Wheeling, he schooled more than 3,000 students on how to embalm and prepare bodies for viewing. And, as important, he worked to make sure they knew to pay attention to the living and show compassion for the needs of the bereaved.</p><p>There are few colleges like Worsham, the launching pad for the careers of many who run funeral homes in the Chicago area and beyond.</p><p>"You name a funeral director in Chicago," said Leili McMurrough, the mortuary school's president. "They were all taught by Tim. Very few people have the privilege of shaping a profession. And Tim did exactly that."</p><p>Mr. Kowalski, who retired in 2024, died May 27. His family did not give the cause of death. He was 75.</p><p>McMurrough said he helped his students focus on the dignity of the deceased and act with reverence.</p><p>"He wouldn't use words like 'tools' while embalming," she said. "It was always 'instruments.' He really took teaching seriously. He wasn't casual about the responsibility of educating future funeral directors. He'd walk in the classroom, and the room would just go quiet because Tim was there."</p><p>Joseph Rago studied under Mr. Kowalski's tutelage at Worsham.</p><p>"This is a profession where you need to know how to handle the most sensitive of times," said Rago, who went on to teach at the school and to operate Rago Brothers Funeral Homes. "And I think Tim was good in instructing that and preparing us for that."</p><p>For many years, working with his students, Mr. Kowalski helped oversee the process of indigent burials in Cook County, handling everything from embalming to graveside prayers.</p><p>In 2011, as the plywood coffins of 24 people who didn't have family members willing or able to pay for a funeral or who had no family were being place in the ground at Memorial Gardens Cemetery in Homewood, Mr. Kowalski offered these words, as Chicago Sun-Times columnist Neil Steinberg reported:</p><p>"We commend to God the souls of these individuals whose mortal remains lie before us and commit their bodies to earth ... We did not know these people. Many things about them will remain always a mystery to us. We do not know what were the circumstances of their lives. Many may have died in poverty. Others might have simply outlived their families. Our beginnings do not know our ends. We do not know any of these things. But one thing we do know, they were human beings. And, at the end of their lives, they deserve to be treated with respect. Our common humanity demands that these lives should not pass from the earth unremembered."</p><p>Nikkia L. Brown was among the Worsham students who helped with the burials that day.</p><p>"I remember Mr. Kowalski kind of handpicked us all to be a part of that, and it was kind of special for me," Brown said. "I was just a girl who was brand new, I wasn't born in the industry, my family isn't involved in funeral homes, it's just me. And it was something that was touching for me. For these people who didn't have family, and we're the last people they encounter, giving them a dignified burial — it was an honor. I consider it sacred. And Mr. Kowalski made that happen."</p><p>Mr. Kowalkski was known to some "Special K" because of his last name and to others as "Cobra" because his exacting standards could sting.</p><p>"He was just one of a kind," said Brown, who operates In Touch Funeral & Cremation Services on the South Side. "He was very humble, but he was also like the GOAT of embalming. And he knew it. And he knew that everyone looked up to him and really valued him."</p><p>Brown said she and other former students occasionally bent Mr. Kowalski's ear with problems as they progressed in their careers.</p><p>Mr. Kowalski, who lived on the Northwest Side, attended the old Weber High School, Loyola University Chicago and Mundelein Seminary. He then served as a Catholic priest but decided to resign active ministry and attend Worsham, working in the funeral industry before beginning his teaching career.</p><p>He loved traveling, Renaissance art, Egyptology, gourmet food and Mary Jane, his wife.</p><p>"He was kind, compassionate and dedicated," his wife said. "He was a professional. He had high standards.</p><p>"I'm a retired Spanish teacher, and sometimes you don't know how you impact lives until you hear the words of your former students. And they knew him and loved him. He was very demanding, and the students always rose to the occasion."</p><p>Services have been held.</p>

caveman that she adopts in hopes of impressing her social circle. The caveman, after becoming a rising star, inspires legendary playwright Eugene O’Neill, played by Offerman, to pen his classic play “The Iceman Cometh.”</p><p>The production is written by a creative team that includes a few Broadway heavy hitters: Jay Reiss, credited here for book and lyrics, is one of the creative minds behind the Tony Award- winning “Twenty Fifth Annual Putnam County Spelling Bee.”<i> </i>Mark Hollmann, also credited for book and lyrics, won a Tony for the music and lyrics of “Urinetown.”</p><p>By all accounts the creative team, which also includes writer Erin Quinn Purcell, describes the musical as a farce with heart. Mullally attributes those characteristics to Hollmann.</p><p>“His melodies are just unbelievable,” she said of Hollman, a native of downstate Fairview Heights. “He's a genius, and some of his melodies are so exquisitely beautiful, but then the very up-tempo, funny songs are also so catchy. entries.title: Revenge of the tan suit at the Obama Presidential Center ceremony
entries.summary: <p>Presidential scandals just hit different in 2014 — we called this one “The Audacity of Taupe.” Then-President Barack Obama was feted as a cool guy with surprisingly good style for a world leader; first lady Michelle Obama had been a fashion icon, and the young family in the White House injected a Camelot-like vibrancy to the notoriously dowdy Washington, D.C. scene.</p><p>Yet when the president <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/lifestyle-fashion-beauty-and-fashion-united-states-government-03a06154e00743cc9e113c51e8273a5f" target="_blank" ><u>emerged on Aug. 28</u></a> to discuss foreign policy, the headlines slipped past the possibility of military action in Syria or tensions between Russia and Ukraine. Obama wore “a beige-colored jacket and a gray, striped tie,” as <a class="Link" href="https://www.politifact.com/article/2014/aug/28/obamas-tan-suit-earns-full-flop/" target="_blank" ><u>PolitiFact put it</u></a>. “Yes we tan!” some wags joked on social media; “Taupe and Change” quipped others. Other commentators dissed the decision to wear a military-adjacent color, given the topic of the press conference; one Republican Congressman called it “unpresidential.” Presidents of both parties <a class="Link" href="https://threadreaderapp.com/thread/1819078797490377186.html?utm_campaign=t" target="_blank" ><u>going back decades</u></a> have worn tan suits, including Ronald Reagan, with no controversy — also before social media and cable news.</p><p>The infamous tan suit became a punchline for years to come, even as some Democratic politicians came to embrace the look, as then-Vice President Kamala Harris did <a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/2024/08/20/style/kamala-harris-dnc-tan-suit.html?unlocked_article_code=1.rFA.vlnr.SH7GhHIorkH-&smid=url-share" target="_blank" ><u>during her own nominating convention</u></a> to the presidency in 2024. The suit itself is not preserved or presented at the Obama Presidential Center, but during the opening ceremony on Thursday, multiple guests and celebrities paid tribute to the look. As for Obama himself, his own verdict on the fit? “Listen, I own that tan suit proudly, brother!” he <a class="Link" href="https://www.facebook.com/share/r/1EGfRx5Aoq/" target="_blank" ><u>recently told</u></a> comedian Stephen Colbert (who is sporting beige himself at the ceremony).</p><p>Here are our favorite tan suits among the crowd at the Obama Presidential Center opening entries.title: Beatrice Lumpkin, workers’ rights leader and 'rock of the movement,' dies at 107
entries.summary: <p>Beatrice Lumpkin wasn't just liberal, or left-leaning, or a secret communist sympathizer. She was an open, enthusiastic, dues-paying member of the Communist Party for nearly 90 years, whose passion for workers' rights put her on the front lines of post-World War II labor struggles in Chicago, from working with Black Panther Fred Hampton to the fight to compensate employees abruptly fired at the closing of the Wisconsin Steel plant in 1980, to the recent unionization of Starbucks employees.</p><p>"Bea was born and grew up and lived her life in the Communist Party," said Roberta Wood, secretary-treasurer of the Communist Party USA.</p><p>Lumpkin, 107, died in Hyde Park, Sunday, June 14.</p><p>Mayor Brandon Johnson, who declared Aug. 3 as "Beatrice Lumpkin Day" in Chicago, called her "a towering figure in the labor movement, an unwavering advocate for fully funded education, and a continued source of inspiration for us all."</p><p>"Spanning almost an entire century of public engagement, Lumpkin was deeply involved in movements for workers' rights, civil rights, and educational justice. She advocated for the right of workers to organize and bargain collectively, supported efforts to advance racial justice, and fought for policies that protected vulnerable communities," Johnson continued, in a statement. </p><p>"As a teacher and organizer, Bea brought the lessons of solidarity into the classroom. As a math teacher in Chicago Public Schools and at Malcolm X College, she inspired generations of students while remaining deeply engaged building worker power. Through her leadership in the Chicago Teachers Union Retiree Committee and Climate Justice Committee, she built bridges between generations, reminding us that strong schools and strong communities are built through collective action and a steadfast commitment to justice." </p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a Chicago. A celebration of her life is being planned for that weekend.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Provided by City of Chicago</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>She was born in New York in 1918. Her parents, Dora and Morris Shapiro, Belarus radicals who emigrated to America after the failed Russian revolution of 1905, ran a laundry. Lumpkin would say she was born "knowing which side I was on." By age 9 she was marching with striking textile workers.</p><p>In her mid-teens, she joined the Young Communist League, and since then, she "never had a moment when there was nothing to do," she wrote in her 2013 autobiography, "Joy in the Struggle: My Life and Love." "There were always picket lines for workers on strike, demonstrations to demand food for a hungry family, knocking on doors to sell The Daily Worker, or bring people out to vote."</p><p></p><p>She went to Hunter College, but found "union work was too important and too exciting" to waste time in school. She later returned and graduated.</p><p>She moved to Buffalo in 1942 to work for Sylvania Radio. There she met a force in the Buffalo Communist movement, Hattie Lumpkin and, more significantly, her son Frank. They married on Oct. 22, 1949.</p><p>"My father was in the Merchant Marines," said their son, John Lumpkin, the former director of the Illinois Department of Public Health. "My grandmother was very active in the people's movement. When he came home from the war, they met at his mother's house and fell in love."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-250000" name="image-250000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/789d5e8/2147483647/strip/true/crop/422x237+0+136/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F2a%2F74%2F1d2b94704775b7d126ba0b5d3c2a%2Ffrank-and-bea.gif 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/f76388d/2147483647/strip/true/crop/422x237+0+136/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F2a%2F74%2F1d2b94704775b7d126ba0b5d3c2a%2Ffrank-and-bea.gif 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/9413d6b/2147483647/strip/true/crop/422x237+0+136/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F2a%2F74%2F1d2b94704775b7d126ba0b5d3c2a%2Ffrank-and-bea.gif" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Married in 1949, Beatrice and Frank Lumpkin were a team fighting for civil rights and workers rights. Frank Lumpkin died in 2010.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Provided.</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>"She and Frank were an extraordinary couple," said Tom Geoghegan, a longtime Chicago labor lawyer who represented the Wisconsin Steel workers. "Frank had a wonderful heart, and she had a great heart too. They each had their own form of courage and complemented each other. They had a real romance."</p><p>The couple settled in Gary, Indiana, and Frank Lumpkin went to work at Wisconsin Steel in 1950.</p><p>In 1965, she became a Chicago Public Schools teacher, then an associate professor at Malcolm X College, originally Crane Junior College, around the time it changed its name, where she focused on stressing the multicultural roots of knowledge. In the 1980s, she contributed to the Portland Model Baseline essays, a comprehensive attempt to highlight Black contributions to every aspect of education.</p><p>"The African contributions to mathematics comprise a vast field of study because it was in Africa that the foundations of our modern mathematics were developed," Lumpkin wrote in one PMB essay. "Since Africa is widely believed to be the birthplace of the human race, it follows that Africa was the birthplace of mathematics and science."</p><p> With Black contributions to society being vigorously scrubbed from history today, Lumpkin reflects the opposite extreme of the spectrum — too far, for some critics, who found her Afrocentrism "keen to deny the Greeks any intellectual achievements of their own."</p><p></p><p>In 1974, she was involved in forming the Coalition of Labor Union Women, serving on its executive board for 20 years. </p><p>On March 28, 1980, Wisconsin Steel closed its doors, firing 3,500 workers. Their last paycheck bounced. Its longtime owner, International Harvester, had sold the mill to Environdyne in 1977, to shed itself of pension obligations. Their union proved feckless and Frank Lumpkin stepped forward and formed the Save Our Jobs Committee.</p><p>"As he put it, it was a question of fight or die," said Beatrice Lumpkin, who aided him in his efforts, later publishing a book about the struggle, "Always Bring a Crowd: The Story of Frank Lumpkin, Steelworker." After a 17-year struggle, the fired Wisconsin Steel workers received nearly $15 million in compensation.</p><p>Survivors include sons John Lumpkin, Paul Lumpkin and Carl Mohrherr, and daughter Jeanleah Mohrherr, as well as three grandchildren and a great-grandson.</p><p>"She was the person who was always showing up, wherever people were demonstrating," said John Lumpkin. "Recently, when folks at Starbucks were out on strike, she was there with them. She was at the No Kings demonstrations. She was a rock of the movement."</p><p>"A lot of people talk about the sacrifices they made for the movement," said Roberta Wood. "For Bea, it was never a sacrifice. It was all the joy of the struggle. She was raised to think your job is to make the world better."</p><p> "She was a heroic woman, an indefatigable organizer and a person who never gave up," said Geoghegan. "What was extraordinary about Bea is she started young and kept marching until the end. She believed in class struggle, and communists were the best people to articulate that. She had a sense of humor about herself as she got older. She was a cheerful person with an extraordinary sense of justice." </p>

entries.title: Daniel Palencia en la lista de lesionados de los Cubs por inflamación en el codo
entries.summary: <p>Ya con tres miembros de su rotación inicial fuera por lesiones, los <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" target="_blank" >Cubs</a> ahora también deben encontrar la forma de vivir sin su cerrador.</p><p>El diestro Daniel Palencia fue colocado en la lista de lesionados por inflamación en el codo el martes, lo que marca su segunda visita a la lista de lesionados (IL) esta temporada. Anteriormente había estado fuera por una lesión en el oblicuo.</p><p>Palencia lanzó en la novena entrada de la <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/06/15/cubs-pete-crow-armstrong-hit-for-cycle-walk-off-win-rockies-pedro-ramirez-matt-shaw-shota-imanaga" target="_blank" >victoria por “walk-off”</a> del lunes, momento en el que recibió una visita en el campo del mánager Craig Counsell y de un entrenador. Permaneció en el juego y ponchó a tres bateadores consecutivos, pero se sintió lo suficientemente mal como para que los Cubs consideraran apropiado colocarlo en la lista de lesionados.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-890000" name="module-890000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>“Después del juego en Colorado [el miércoles pasado], no se sentía bien”, explicó Counsell el martes. “Tuvimos cuatro días de descanso entre salidas. Se recuperó bien y se sintió bien antes del juego de anoche”.</p><p>“Sólo estaba preocupado porque el lenguaje corporal no era normal. [Durante la visita en la loma], dijo que estaba bien, pero luego presentó síntomas y el codo no se sentía bien; hoy tampoco”.</p><p>Cuando se le preguntó si los Cubs habrían terminado en la misma situación si Palencia hubiera sido retirado del juego, Counsell coincidió en que sí.</p><p>“El pitcher dijo: ‘Estoy bien, estoy bien’. Y ponchó a los tres siguientes después de eso. Pero por precaución, tiene sentido incluirlo en la lista”, dijo el martes el presidente del equipo, Jed Hoyer. “Ciertamente, cuando un mánager sale por esa razón, muchas veces [el jugador también] sale. Él insistió en que se sentía genial y se reafirmó en eso lanzando muy bien después de eso”.</p><p>“Pero dadas las conversaciones después del juego, tuvo sentido ponerlo en la lista”, agregó.</p><p>Counsell dijo que no hay estimación de cuánto tiempo estarán los Cubs sin su cerrador, quien se destacó como un arma de alto octanaje en la novena entrada la temporada pasada, cuando salvó 22 juegos y terminó la campaña con una efectividad de 2.91.</p><p>Esa efectividad es aún más baja esta temporada, con 2.70 en 19 apariciones de relevista. Pero pasar casi un mes entre salidas, desde el 12 de abril hasta el 5 de mayo, debido a la lesión en el oblicuo y al récord de 12-23 de los Cubs en sus últimos 35 juegos, ha convertido las oportunidades de salvamento en algo raro, con Palencia logrando solo tres salvamentos.</p><p>Los Cubs tendrán que seguir haciendo lo que han estado haciendo en la parte de pitcheo y buscar alternativas.</p><p>En la rotación —donde Cade Horton, Matthew Boyd, Justin Steele y Jameson Taillon aún están en la lista de lesionados y Edward Cabrera salió temprano con el entrenador el martes por la noche— esa estrategia <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/06/12/cubs-starting-pitching-injuries-depth-rotation-javier-assad-tommy-hottovy-matthew-boyd-jameson-taillon-cade-horton-colin-rea" target="_blank" >ha dado resultados mixtos</a>. Ahora depende de un grupo de relevistas, muchos de los cuales también han lidiado con lesiones y luchas en el campo esta temporada, para llenar el vacío dejado por Palencia cuando surjan las oportunidades de salvamento.</p><p>“Los muchachos tendrán que conseguir sus outs”, dijo Counsell. “Quizás no sea el mismo orden todas las noches, pero serán los mismos chicos, solo en diferentes órdenes”.</p><p>Si bien los Cubs llegaron el martes con una efectividad en el bullpen más baja esta temporada (3.63) que el año pasado (3.78), la necesidad de reemplazar a Palencia surge un día después de que dos veteranos tuvieron problemas en las entradas finales. Phil Maton golpeó a un bateador y otorgó una carrera por base por bolas, y Caleb Thielbar permitió un jonrón de tres carreras en la victoria del lunes.</p><p>La vida sin Palencia puede que no sea tan fácil, pero el tiempo dirá.</p><p>Una curiosidad más: ¿Cuánto, si es que acaso, podría haber tenido que ver el hecho de que Palencia <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/03/18/cubs-reliever-daniel-palencia-is-on-top-of-the-world-counsell-venezuela-wbc" target="_blank" >estuvo lanzando para Venezuela en el Clásico Mundial de Béisbol</a> con sus lesiones?.</p><p>“¿Quién sabe? No lo sé, no hay manera de probar o refutar eso”, comentó Hoyer. “Hablamos en su momento de que no era lo más cómodo para los Cubs, ni para los Brewers; había muchos equipos que se vieron afectados por el calendario, diría yo. Pero no hay manera de probar ni refutar eso”.</p><p>“Es un aumento inusual para los muchachos, es un tiempo inusual para hacer lo que están haciendo. Y cuando los muchachos se lesionan o no rinden bien al comienzo de la temporada, la gente se hace esas preguntas. No hay manera de saber qué causa eso, pero es algo que la gente va a preguntar, y entiendo por qué lo preguntan”.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (AI) y editado por </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a></p>
